subject: Critical Thinking
title: What Is a Logical Fallacy?
description: Learn What Is a Logical Fallacy? in one minute.

hook.text: An argument can sound persuasive, feel logical, and still be completely wrong. That's a fallacy.

buildup.text: A logical fallacy is a flaw in reasoning that undermines an argument's logic — regardless of whether the conclusion is true.

discovery.text: Aristotle cataloged 13 fallacies in 350 BC. Two millennia later, we've identified over 100 — and still fall for them.

twist.text: A fallacy doesn't mean the conclusion is wrong. It means the reasoning doesn't support it.

climax.text: Fallacies persist because they mimic good reasoning. They're convincing — that's what makes them dangerous.

punchline.text: Bad logic can reach good conclusions. That's the trap.

quiz.question: What does a logical fallacy mean about a conclusion?
options: The reasoning doesn't support it, but it could still be true
The argument was made in bad faith

details.summary: A logical fallacy is an error in reasoning that undermines an argument's validity. Fallacies may be formal (structural flaws) or informal (content flaws), and both can make invalid arguments feel convincing.
details.whyItMatters: Fallacies are persuasive precisely because they mimic good reasoning. Recognizing them is the most practical critical thinking skill you can develop.
takeaways: Fallacies are errors in reasoning, not factual mistakes
They can be formal (structural) or informal (content-based)
Persuasive power often hides the logical flaw

faq.question: What is the difference between a formal and an informal fallacy?
faq.answer: A formal fallacy has a flaw in its logical structure regardless of content. An informal fallacy has correct structure but misleading content, such as irrelevant premises or ambiguous language. Both produce invalid conclusions.

faq.question: Why are logical fallacies so difficult to spot in real time?
faq.answer: Fallacies often sound reasonable because they mimic valid reasoning patterns or exploit emotional responses. Detecting them requires deliberate analysis that conflicts with our natural tendency toward fast, intuitive processing.
